hook.text: Decide what you'll test before you look at the data. Good advice... but how do you know what to test, without looking?

bills.text: Here are two hundred and forty-four restaurant bills, and the tip left on each one.

days.text: Split them by day, and Friday tips best, at seventeen percent... against fifteen on Saturday.

few.text: But only nineteen of these bills are from a Friday. A group that small wobbles a lot.

median.text: Swap the average for the median, and Sunday wins instead.

lead.text: So this isn't a finding. It's a lead... a question worth asking properly.

jobs-in.text: Which means there are two different jobs here.

jobs.text: Exploring is roaming the data, slicing it every way you can. What comes out is questions, never conclusions.

confirm.text: Confirming is stating ONE hypothesis in advance, and testing it once, on data nobody has looked at. What comes out is a claim.

sin.text: Keep a wall between them. The trap is crossing it, by testing a lead on the data that suggested it. Friday was picked because it looked best in these very bills... so the test is tilted its way before it runs.

lie.text: A p-value from the data that suggested the question is a lie.

split-in.text: So where does the fresh data come from?

split.text: If you can't collect more, split what you have before you explore. Seventy percent to roam in... and thirty locked away.

carry.text: When a lead turns up, carry the question across the wall, but not the data.

once.text: Then test it once, on bills that never had a say in the hunch. Whatever that says is the answer.

ab-in.text: Or better still, make fresh data on purpose.

design.text: That's an A/B test: an experiment where almost everything is decided before the first user arrives.

hypothesis.text: One hypothesis. The new checkout button raises the conversion rate.

metric.text: And one metric to judge it by, chosen now. Track ten and cheer whichever one moves, and you're back to p-hacking.

who-in.text: Then comes the step that makes it an experiment.

who.text: Who sees which button? Let users choose, and the two groups differ before the test even starts.

traits.text: Here's how far apart they sit on ten traits. Age, income, prior use... and two a real test never sees, like motivation.

coin.text: Flip a coin for each user instead, and every gap shrinks to noise. Even the two nobody measured.

cause.text: The coin doesn't know what it's balancing, so it balances everything. That's what lets a test say the button CAUSED the change.

size-in.text: Two more decisions, before anyone clicks.

size.text: How many users? To catch ten percent rising to twelve, with eighty percent power, you need about three thousand eight hundred per arm.

peek.text: And no peeking. Here's another test, with both arms identical. There's nothing to find.

wander.text: Recompute its p-value after every hundred visitors, and it wanders... dipping under point oh five, twice.

stop.text: Stop at the first dip, and you've shipped noise. At the planned eight thousand, it reads point one nine.

result-in.text: So set the number, and look once, at the end.

result.text: Here's a finished test, with six thousand users in each arm.

counts.text: Five hundred and seventy-nine bought with the old button. Seven hundred and two with the new.

lift.text: That's nine point six five percent against eleven point seven. A lift of two points... about a fifth more sales.

interval.text: Its ninety-five percent interval runs from about one point to three, and the p-value is three in ten thousand.

four.text: Report all four together: the lift, its interval, the p-value, and an effect size. Never the p-value alone.

decide.text: Then decide, on two questions. Is it significant? Yes. The whole interval sits above zero.

matter.text: And is it big enough to matter? That one's about money, not math.

tiny.text: A big enough test makes even eight percent rising to eight point oh two significant. It's real... and worthless.

permit.text: Significance gives you permission to look at the size. It doesn't tell you to ship.

began.text: This course began with two groups, a gap between them, and one question. Could this just be luck?

since.text: Everything since has been a way to answer it honestly.

last.text: So look all you like. Then decide the question... and ask it once, of data that hasn't answered it yet.

wobble.text: Its average could be anywhere from fifteen to nineteen percent, overlapping every other day.

luck.text: Part of its lead is luck, and the test would count that luck as evidence.

verdict.text: Here, the lift could be as little as one point. Ship it only if one point is worth it.
